scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Internet traffic from all internal users became slower and
sometimes flaky. Active TCP connections kept working but new
connections to 203.0.113.x sometimes time out then succeed.
R1 reports it lost an OSPF neighbor. Identify which.

injection.action: kill ospfd on ISPA (primary internet default-originator)

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: ispa ospfd daemon
Mechanism: Both ISPA and ISPB advertise a default route into
  the OSPF domain via `default-information originate`. R1
  prefers ISPA (lower cost). When ISPA's ospfd dies, R1
  ages out the default learned from ISPA and falls back to
  ISPB's default. During the timeout + reconvergence window,
  new connections fail. Once converged on ISPB, service
  resumes but takes a slightly different path.
Localization: ispa
Root cause: ospfd not running on ispa
Fix: `/etc/init.d/frr restart` on ispa

Observable note (lab-verified 2026-07-03): ospfd is killed together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it. vtysh remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO `router ospf` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists ospfd. An agent may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the ospf configuration is missing/empty on ispa" -- that is the same fault observed at the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The fault is on ispa: its ospfd process has crashed and been left in a failed
state. Watchfrr on ispa is also dead, so there is no automatic restart.
The frr.service on ispa shows "inactive (dead)" even though /etc/frr/daemons
has ospfd=yes and frr.conf contains a complete OSPF configuration.

Mechanism: ispa and ispb are supposed to form an OSPF adjacency over the
192.0.2.0/30 link (ispa.eth1 ↔ ispb.eth1). When running normally, each
redistributes its connected routes into OSPF. Critically, ispa carries
several simulated internet loopbacks (66.235.200.145, 152.250.31.93,
172.253.62.100, 216.239.35.0) and ispb carries its own internet loopback
(216.239.35.4). With OSPF up, ispa learns 216.239.35.4/32 from ispb and
installs a specific route via 192.0.2.2; without it, ispa's only route for
that prefix is its kernel default (via 203.0.113.2 — R1). This creates a
forwarding loop: packets destined for ispb's loopback travel
R1 → ispa → R1 → ispa … until TTL expires. Connections to ispa's own
loopbacks still succeed; connections to ispb's address consistently time out
and may succeed only on retry if the client reaches a working destination.
This asymmetric reachability is the "sometimes time out then succeed" pattern
and explains the overall internet degradation reported by all internal users.

Localization: the fault is entirely on ispa. ispb's ospfd is running and
healthy (7 external LSAs queued, watchfrr active), but it has zero OSPF
neighbors because ispa's ospfd is dead. The "lost OSPF neighbor" is ispa,
as reported by ispb losing its only expected adjacency.

Root cause: ispa's ospfd was killed and watchfrr was also stopped, leaving
the OSPF process permanently down with no self-healing.

Corrective fix: on ispa, run `systemctl start frr` (or `service frr start`)
to bring ospfd back up. The OSPF adjacency with ispb will reform within
one Hello interval (10 s), route exchange will complete, and the routing loop
for 216.239.35.4 will be eliminated. No configuration change is needed —
the frr.conf on ispa is correct.

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly identifies ispa as the affected device with ospfd crashed and watchfrr dead.
The report explicitly names ospfd/OSPF as crashed and explains the lost OSPF adjacency and routing impact.

The writeup never explains the R1 default-route failover (that R1 prefers ISPA's default and only falls back to ISPB's default after ISPA's OSPF dies/ages out), so it doesn't explain the ISPB failover behavior required by the axis.
Recommends starting the frr service on ispa (systemctl start/service start), which will restore ospfd and reestablish the OSPF adjacency as required.

The agent's investigation log contains direct observations (ospfd failed on ispa, watchfrr dead, frr.conf present, routing tables showing default via R1 and routes via R1 causing a loop) that support the final diagnosis and proposed fix. The reasoning links those observations to a forwarding loop and explains why service intermittently fails, with no critical gaps.
